reason: The passage depicts bold and open expression of views rather than discouragement thereof. Elijah speaks directly and confrontationally to King Ahab multiple times, publicly addresses the assembled people ('וַיִּגַּ֨שׁ אֵלִיָּ֜הוּ אֶל־ כָּל־ הָעָ֗ם וַיֹּ֙אמֶר֙'), and explicitly invites the people to make and voice their own judgment ('עַד־ מָתַ֞י אַתֶּ֣ם פֹּסְחִים־ עַל־ שְׁתֵּ֣י הַסְּעִפִּים'). While the text mentions Jezebel's suppression of prophets, it shows active resistance to that suppression rather than widespread discouragement of expression. The narrative arc demonstrates public prophecy, direct confrontation with authority, and communal deliberation as normalized practices.
